title: Africa: Indigenous Grain Beers, Honey Wine & Palm Wine
attribution: Africa's indigenous ferments — sorghum and millet opaque beers, Ethiopian honey wine, palm wine — predate and stand apart from European brewing traditions. Most have no statutory definition; a few (Ethiopian tej, industrial sorghum beer) are commercially produced. Documented from ethnographic and food-science sources; values are typical.

styles.name: Umqombothi / Sorghum Beer
styles.impression: Southern Africa's traditional beer: thick, sour, opaque and still actively fermenting when drunk — pinkish-brown, gritty, and sipped from a shared clay pot.
styles.comments: Central to Xhosa and Zulu ritual — weddings, funerals, ancestral ceremonies. The lactic sourness and low alcohol are defining; it is as much food as drink. Industrially produced as 'Chibuku' shake-shake in cartons.
styles.ingredients: Maize meal and sorghum malt, soured by lactic fermentation then alcohol-fermented by wild yeast. Left unfiltered and drunk live.

styles.name: Pito / Burukutu / Dolo
styles.impression: West Africa's sorghum and millet beers — cloudy, tart and dark, brewed by (usually women) and sold fresh at markets.
styles.comments: Pito (Ghana, Nigeria), dolo (Burkina Faso), burukutu (Nigeria). Drunk warm and fresh from calabashes within a day or two.
styles.ingredients: Malted sorghum or millet, mashed, soured and fermented with wild yeast and a pitched portion of a previous brew.
styles.tags: africa, sorghum, millet, pito, dolo, traditional

styles.name: Tella / Injera-Grain Beer (ጠላ)
styles.impression: Ethiopia's homebrewed grain beer — smoky, tart and dark, flavoured with gesho (buckthorn) as the bittering agent in place of hops.
styles.comments: Gesho is Africa's closest analogue to hops — a bittering, preserving plant. Tella is the everyday house beer; a stronger, filtered version exists for guests.
styles.ingredients: Roasted barley, wheat or other grain with gesho (Rhamnus prinoides) leaves and twigs, fermented in a clay pot; the vessel is often smoked with olivewood.

styles.name: Tej / Berz (ጠጅ)
styles.impression: Ethiopian and Eritrean honey wine — sweet, cloudy, deceptively strong, and bittered with gesho. The ancestral drink of the Ethiopian court.
styles.comments: Served in a rounded flask (berele). Strength varies wildly with fermentation time and honey ratio. A defining feature is the gesho bittering, which links it to tella.
styles.ingredients: Honey and water fermented with wild yeast, bittered with gesho (Rhamnus prinoides). Berz is the young, near-non-alcoholic stage.

styles.name: Palm Wine (Emu / Nsafufuo / Matango)
styles.impression: Tapped palm sap that ferments spontaneously into a sweet, effervescent, milky wine within hours — sweeter fresh, sourer and stronger as the day goes on.
styles.comments: Drunk across West and Central Africa (and the tropics worldwide). Central to ceremony — marriage, naming, libation. Distilled it becomes ogogoro / akpeteshie.
styles.ingredients: Sap of oil, raffia or coconut palms, collected from the felled or standing tree; wild yeast ferments it immediately.

styles.name: Akpeteshie / Ogogoro (Distilled Palm Spirit)
styles.impression: West Africa's distilled palm spirit — fiery, raw and potent, long outlawed under colonial rule and now a proud local spirit.
styles.comments: Akpeteshie (Ghana), ogogoro (Nigeria). Banned by colonial authorities protecting imported liquor; became a symbol of independence.
